notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 8 from the sources I could open. A few gaps first:

- **Missing sources:** I couldn't find NET Bible notes or anything from Orthodox sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm.
- **Catholic view:** this rests only on short search snippets of Augustine's exposition. I couldn't open the full page.
- **Thin verses:** I found nothing specific on v. 9, and very little on vv. 7–8.

Labels like "Methodist" or "Lutheran" refer to each commentator's own background, as StudyLight or the site itself identifies it.

---

**Title ("According to Gittith")**
- **Meaning unknown:** A Lutheran writer at 1517.org says no one knows what "on the Gittith" means—perhaps "winepress" or, as Lyra and Luther both imagined, a musical instrument. https://www.1517.org/articles/psalm-8-from-the-mouth-of-babes-why-do-you-care-o-lord
- **Guzik's reading:** He takes it as "the instrument of Gath," which tells us the sound of the psalm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **Spurgeon:** Some trace the word to a song for treading grapes. Since it also heads Psalms 81 and 84, both joyful, he concludes it marks a hymn of delight. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps008.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** His title reads "for the wine-presses." He notes the psalm never mentions winepresses, so he takes them as a picture of the Churches, on the same principle by which we understand also by a threshing-floor the Church. In the Church, God's ministers separate the good from the worldly, as juice is pressed from husks. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801008.htm

**v. 1**
- **"LORD, our Lord":** Guzik says David puts God's covenant name (LORD) beside His role as Master of His people (Lord). In effect: "Our God is our Master." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **God of all nations:** Guzik adds that the LORD is Israel's covenant God but also more than Israel's, since His name is excellent "in all the earth." Even the earth can't measure His glory, which is "above the heavens." (same URL)
- **Spurgeon's preaching hints:** "Our Lord" means claiming the Lord personally as ours. "In all the earth" points to God revealing Himself everywhere in nature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps008.cfm

**v. 2: the most debated verse**
- **"Strength" or "praise"?** The Hebrew word means strength. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has "praise," and Matthew 21:16 quotes it that way, as do the Latin Vulgate and the Syriac (Barnes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-2.htm
  - Ellicott: Because the verse uses the language of war, he leans toward the word's original sense of a stronghold or defence. (same URL)
  - Maclaren: God builds a fortress out of children's speech, like some border castle, that holds back the enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-2.html
- **Who are the "babes"? Readings differ:**
  - *Literal children:* Calvin (Reformed) says that even if every adult fell silent, the speechless mouths of infants could still praise God. Clarke (Methodist) sees in infants enough evidence for God to silence every atheist. The Pulpit Commentary means small children just able to lisp God's praise. Maclaren sees no good reason to take the words other than naturally. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-2.html
  - *The apostles and early believers:* Gill (Baptist) rejects the literal reading. He takes the babes as the apostles and first preachers of the Gospel, and the "strength" as the gospel itself. (same URL)
  - *Weak people God uses:* Barnes thinks it means people as feeble as infants whom God uses to overthrow His enemies. He doubts that children's instinctive wonder is the point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-2.htm
  - *Several layers at once:* Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) sees God's glory here in nature, in providence, and in Christ's kingdom. That kingdom advanced through poor fishermen, and children cried "Hosanna" when the priests rejected Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_008.cfm
- **Lutheran:** The 1517.org writer notes Luther's point that this power is ordained through the mouth, not the hand or the sword. https://www.1517.org/articles/psalm-8-from-the-mouth-of-babes-why-do-you-care-o-lord
- **Guzik and Spurgeon:**
  - Guzik ties the verse to God using weak things (1 Cor 1:27).
  - He says that in Matthew 21:16 Jesus identified Himself as God and His angry critics as the "enemy and avenger."
  - Spurgeon pictures the adversary shamed by being struck down by infants. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
  - Spurgeon also preached a whole sermon on God's power shown in human weakness. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/god-glorified-by-childrens-mouths
- **Who is the "enemy and avenger"?**
  - Gill: Satan, whose power God has "caused to cease." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/psalms/8-2.html
  - Another note on Bible Hub: someone who grabs for himself the right to judge, which belongs to God alone (Deut 32:35). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-2.htm
- **Devotional:** The Bible Hub verse page calls praise "God's chosen weapon," available to every believer from the cradle on. https://biblehub.com/psalms/8-2.htm

**v. 3**
- **Looking up:** Guzik stresses the value of simply looking at the night sky. He notes Clarke's wonder that stars bigger than the sun are only "the work of God's fingers." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **Starting with God:** Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says philosophers ask "What is man?" but start with man, while David starts with God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/psalms-8.html
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** No sane person can look at the night sky without sensing God and our need of Him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/psalms-8.html

**v. 4**
- **Not doubt, but wonder:** Guzik notes David never doubts that God is mindful of man. He only wonders why. Kidner says the same question elsewhere can mock pride (Ps 144), plead in suffering (Job 7) or shudder at sin (Job 25), but here it is pure astonishment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **Fallen or created man?**
  - Matthew Poole (Puritan) and Adam Clarke (Methodist) take *enosh* as frail man in his fallen state of sin and death. Clarke reads "son of man" as son of Adam, the fallen child of a fallen parent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-4.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-4.html
  - Ellicott: the first word may suggest frailty, the second human descent. The answer must hold together our frailty and our glorious destiny. https://biblehub.com/psalms/8-4.htm
  - Barnes: The point is that nothing in man earned this honor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-4.htm
- **"Visit" or "care for":** Guzik says "visit" is stronger than "mindful": God thinks about us and acts in our lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/ Coffman links God's "visiting" to the Dayspring from on high visiting us (Luke 1:78). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-4.html
- **Pointing to Christ:** GotQuestions says Psalm 8:4 was fulfilled in Jesus Christ, citing Hebrews 2. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-is-man-that-you-are-mindful-of-him.html Augustus Toplady (Anglican, on Monergism) wrote a full sermon on this verse. https://www.monergism.com/gods-mindfulness-man-psalm-84

**v. 5: "angels" or "God"?**
- **The Hebrew word:** It is *elohim*, "God" or "gods." The Aramaic paraphrase, Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac and Hebrews 2:7 all render it "angels" (Barnes). Gesenius renders it "but little lower than God," and Barnes calls that the more natural reading. Still, he grants that the ancient versions and Hebrews make "angels" a proper meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-5.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/8-5.html
- **Ellicott:** The word covers angels as well as God, but nothing in the context limits it to angels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/8-5.htm
- **Coffman:** Older translations were too influenced by the Septuagint, which mistranslated it as "angels." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-5.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** He renders it "lessened him for a little time from God." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/8-5.html
- **Guzik:** He notes Boice reads "lower than God," but prefers "angels" because the Greek translators and Hebrews read it that way. Following Kidner, he says "a little" can mean "for a little while." The destiny of the redeemed is to be lifted above the angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **Lutheran:** The 1517.org writer follows Luther in reading it as "lower *by God*" and applies it to Christ. Jesus is not a lesser copy of God. https://www.1517.org/articles/psalm-8-from-the-mouth-of-babes-why-do-you-care-o-lord
- **Crowned with glory:**
  - Boice (cited by Guzik): the crown links man with God, reflecting His glory as no other creature does.
  - Guzik notes that, as Hebrews says, this dominion looks unfulfilled in fallen man, "but we see Jesus." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
  - Matthew Henry: Christ was exalted and crowned because He humbled Himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_008.cfm

**v. 6**
- **Dominion from creation:** Guzik ties this to the mandate in Genesis 1:26–28 and 9:2. He says dominion means wise, responsible stewardship. It is wrong to see man as merely part of the ecosystem, and wrong to abuse it, since creation belongs to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **Representatives:** GotQuestions says that from the beginning God made humans His representatives, ruling over other creatures in His name. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-is-man-that-you-are-mindful-of-him.html
- **Lutheran:** Christ, made man for us, now rules over all things. Only in His kingdom does God's original purpose for creation finally come true. https://www.1517.org/articles/psalm-8-from-the-mouth-of-babes-why-do-you-care-o-lord

**vv. 7–8**
- **Genesis echoes:** Boice (cited by Guzik) calls the allusions to Genesis 1 "inescapable." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-8/
- **A spiritual reading:** An older note in Spurgeon's *Treasury* reads the animals symbolically: whoever rules the material world is also Lord of the spiritual creation it pictures. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps008.cfm

**Whole psalm: Christ-centred readings**
- **Spurgeon's *Treasury*:** Quoted notes there treat the psalm as a prophetic anticipation of the kingdom of Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps008.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** The New Testament applies the psalm to Christ and the redemption He accomplished. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_008.cfm
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** As Christ suffered and was then exalted, so are we in Him. https://www.1517.org/articles/psalm-8-from-the-mouth-of-babes-why-do-you-care-o-lord
